extracted.intended_audience: advanced mathematics students, mathematicians, and philosophers of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to formulate, test, defend, and revise mathematical conjectures, proofs, and definitions — especially how to treat counterexamples, modify lemmas, and avoid ad hoc redefinitions. Emphasizes proof as a heuristic/thought-experiment and the dialectical process of discovery in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as a thought-experiment / quasi-experiment (decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a 'proof' as a thought-experiment (or 'quasi-experiment') which suggests a decomposition of the original conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas, embedding it in a possibly distant body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher proposes calling 'proof' a thought-experiment that decomposes the conjecture (e.g. embedding the Euler conjecture in the theory of rubber sheets). This clarifies that such a 'proof' may not guarantee truth but provides a structured analysis (lemmas) that can be tested and improved. Historical label: 'quasi-experiment'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check every lemma — don't assume triviality of steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof built from steps/lemmas must have each lemma scrutinized; apparently trivial steps (e.g. 'you can always flatten the surface' or 'triangulate and removing triangles preserves V-E+F') may be false in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cauchy-style thought-experiment for Euler used three steps; pupils raise doubts about each step (flattening, triangulation increasing E and F one-for-one, triangle-removal patterns). The remedy is to test each lemma and not treat plausibility as proof. Local counterexamples often target lemmas, showing they must be corrected or proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish local vs global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'local counterexample' refutes a lemma (subconjecture) without necessarily refuting the main conjecture; a 'global counterexample' refutes the main conjecture itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local-but-not-global counterexamples are criticisms of the proof (its lemmas) but not of the conjecture (e.g. removing an interior triangle that removes no edge/vertex falsifies a lemma about triangle removal but not Euler's formula for the cube). Global counterexamples (e.g. hollow nested cubes giving V-E+F=4) falsify the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples as objective criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples are objective tests that cannot be dismissed by mere suspicion; they must be taken seriously as criticism of lemmas, proofs, definitions, or the conjecture itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue stresses that conjectures cannot ignore counterexamples; suspicion is not criticism, but a counterexample is. Once presented, counterexamples force either proof-revision, definitional clarification, or conjecture-rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve proofs by replacing/refining refuted lemmas (local patching)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lemma is refuted (locally), one acceptable response is to replace it with a slightly modified lemma that avoids the counterexample and re-establish the proof's chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: change 'remove any triangle' to 'remove boundary triangles' to evade a local counterexample; but such patches must be honest (not surreptitious 'I meant...') and their plausibility/existence must be defensible. Repeated local patching can lead to sophisticated conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require constructive existence or explicit method when lemma asserts existence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a lemma asserts the existence of a constructive object or ordering (e.g. an order of triangle removals that preserves the invariant), the proof must provide or indicate how to construct it; merely asserting existence without method undermines the thought-experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kappa's objection: saying 'triangles can be so numbered' is insufficient without a method to construct such numbering; without constructive guidance the thought-experiment 'proof' disappears. Existence claims should be made explicit or proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about domain and intended extensions (define terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g. of 'polyhedron', 'polygon', 'edge', 'face') must be made explicit and agreed upon because the meaning chosen determines whether counterexamples are legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many disputes in the dialogue hinge on competing definitions (solid vs surface polyhedron, polygon vs star-polygon, edges with zero/one vertices). To make counterexamples objective you must agree on the extension of the key terms; otherwise refutations can be evaded by definitional shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monster-barring (ad hoc redefinition) as a primary response
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting counterexamples by ad hoc redefinition of terms to exclude them — 'monster-barring' — is an illegitimate avoidance strategy because it exorcises criticism rather than learning from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delta's method of monster-barring (tightening definitions to exclude nested cubes, twins, urchins, picture-frames, etc.) can save a theorem by fiat but is criticized: it often rests on ad hoc, retrospective clauses and prevents respectful treatment of counterexamples. The dialogue recommends treating counterexamples with respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender method: accept global counterexamples and abandon the conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: If a genuine global counterexample stands and cannot be remedied by proof-fixing, one legitimate option is to abandon/surrender the conjecture and seek a radically new approach or revised conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gamma urges surrender when the conjecture is globally falsified; teacher acknowledges it as a valid method (method of surrender) contrasting it with monster-barring or mere defense of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of defining the property as part of the definition to avoid falsification (Def. P / 'perfect definition')
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaring the conjectured property itself as part of the definition of the object (e.g. defining 'polyhedron' so that V-E+F=2 holds by definition) is an anti-pattern: it forecloses investigation and converts empirical/mathematical problem into mere convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alpha's sarcastic 'Def P' (define polyhedron so Euler's relation holds) would make disputes vanish but is considered illegitimate because it defeats the purpose of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that anomalies/monsters can be fruitful ('hopeful monsters')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some counterexamples or 'monsters' that initially look pathological can stimulate theory-change and lead to valuable extensions or new concepts; anomalies deserve study, not always exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue notes the historiographical fact that monsters (e.g. star-polyhedra, twin tetrahedra) have sometimes led to new concepts and fruitful lines of research; the 'hopeful monster' idea cautions against reflexive monster-barring.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and preserve the invariant operations clearly when using transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof uses transformations or operations (e.g. cutting a face, flattening, triangulating, removing triangles) to show an invariant holds, the proof must state which operations are allowed and why the invariant is preserved under them for all admissible objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy's method required that V, E, F not change under deformation, triangulation, and triangle-removal; pupils found counterexamples where these operations fail to preserve the claimed pattern unless additional conditions (boundary triangles, removal order) are specified and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept heuristic precedence: conjecture can legitimately precede proof
rubrics_metrics.description: In heuristic or discovery order, conjectures often come before proofs; proofs may be sought for already suspected truths and a proof-heuristic can guide which problems to attempt to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos (and historical figures cited) emphasize that theorem-guessing is natural and necessary in mathematics: 'You have to guess a mathematical theorem before you prove it.' Proofs then serve to decompose and analyze conjectures, not always to provide final, immutable truth at first attempt.
